newsitem.title: CHINA: Rival Koreas unable to agree on food aid shipment.
newsitem.headline: Rival Koreas unable to agree on food aid shipment.

text.p: Food aid talks between cold-war rivals Seoul and Pyongyang stalled on Saturday over differences on the amount of grain to be shipped from South Korea to the famine-threatened North and other issues, Seoul officials said.

Pyongyang wanted more than the 40,000 tonnes of food Seoul had offered to deliver before the end of July, and the two sides also disagreed on how the aid should be shipped, through which ports and how it would be labelled, they said.

"Most parts of the proposals have been agreed, but some parts of the proposals have not... so the two parties will meet again tomorrow," said Chang Moon-ik, spokesman of the South Korean embassy in Beijing.

Basic agreement had been reached on the aid shipment, Chang said, adding that negotiators from the Red Cross societies of the two Koreas were expected to reach final agreement during their third day of talks in Beijing on Sunday.
"We think we can make a compromise tomorrow," he told reporters in the Chinese capital after a second session of talks on Saturday failed to close the gap between North and South.
George Weber, Secretary General of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), said on Thursday he hoped the two sides would make progress.
While ethnic Korean residents in China who have visited the North have reported widespread starvation there, Weber said Pyongyang remained in a "pre-famine situation".

Capitalist Seoul and communist Pyongyang have been technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean conflict ended in a truce, and decades of mutual mistrust have made even basic food aid a delicate diplomatic affair.
Inter-Korean Red Cross talks earlier this month in Beijing failed after Seoul declined to say exactly how much aid it would supply to its Stalinist neighbour.

South Korea later promised to ship $8 million worth of corn, flour, powdered milk and instant noodles to the North by the end of July, but details of how to transport, package and distribute the aid remained unresolved.

Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross delegation, had been pushing northern counterparts to accept direct transport through the town of Panmunjom on the highly militarised border between the two Koreas, Chang said.

North Korea, which takes self-reliance as its guiding ideology, has sought to limit any direct contact involved in taking southern grain, while Seoul wants to maximise exchanges and to make sure its aid is clearly labelled as such.

Pyongyang had accepted that donated instant noodles would not be taken out of their labelled packets before distribution, but food labelled as coming from South Korea's Red Cross remained an issue, Chang said.

While the 40,000 tonnes of aid promised by Seoul is dwarfed by aid pledged by other donors -- the European Commission said on Friday it was sending 155,000 tonnes of food -- it could lead to further shipments from the prosperous South.

The situation in the isolated north Asian nation, which has seen a long-term economic decline compounded by two years of disastrous flooding, had become highly unstable, the European Commission's top envoy to Seoul said on Saturday.
"The situation is very explosive," Tue Rohrsted told a news conference. "Nobody knows whether it will explode or implode."
